vignette: Thomas Brennan was driving his campaign SUV along a rain-slicked overpass when a delivery truck drifted across the median. The side-impact crumpled the passenger door and pinned him against the steering wheel. He remembers the collision not as a continuous sequence but as a series of abrupt snapshots: the shattering glass catching the dashboard lights, the sudden violence of his own torso jerking forward, and the quiet, heavy moment afterward when his breath caught in his ribs. When first responders pried the door open, the sharp, sweet odor of spilled alcohol from a broken cooler in the other vehicle flooded the cabin. For months afterward, the exact spots in his lower back and left ribs ached without warning, as though the injury had never settled. Over the following weeks, these fragments began to surface at unpredictable intervals. Thomas found himself unable to reconstruct what had happened when he tried to explain the crash to his wife or his chief of staff; he would lose the thread mid-sentence, certain that the narrative was slipping through his hands. Alongside that difficulty, he developed a steady sense of physical discomfort in his chest and abdomen, which he could not quite locate or ease. When a television commercial showed two cars wrapped around a lamppost, his breath caught and the familiar ache in his ribs flared hot and immediate. If a donor event featured a heavy pour of red wine or a cooler of beer, the smell of alcohol made him step outside onto the pavement, standing there long after the crowd had moved indoors, trying to breathe through the sudden wave of nausea. His daily work as a state legislator became a landscape of parallel disruptions. He could no longer sit in the back of a sedan to the capitol building, nor could he allow a driver to take him to district fundraisers. He relied on staff to arrange every ride, watching other vehicles on the interstate with a quiet dread that made his hands tighten on his briefcase. He had come to believe that the accident had happened to him because of the sort of person he was, and he found himself repeatedly dwelling on what he had done wrong, tracing his steps backward through committee schedules and routing choices until the guilt became a constant companion. What frightened him most was the quiet. An unexpected silence in the legislative hallway—a halted conversation, a paused typist, a momentary lull in the chamber—would instantly make him feel that something dangerous was about to happen. He kept his eyes on the room, scanning exits and faces, certain that he had to remain on guard at all times. During budget briefings, his concentration fractured; he would read the same policy paragraph four times, unable to hold the details in his mind. He felt as though the crash were written on his posture and his expression, and he braced himself every time a journalist or constituent looked at him, convinced they could see what had happened just by watching his hands and his eyes. Now, at sixty-eight, Thomas has spent three years navigating a career that demands steady presence and constant movement. His avoidance of vehicles has required his wife to reroute their entire social calendar, and the difficulty concentrating has left amended bills sitting unfinished on his desk. What finally brought him to the clinic was a tremor in his forearms during a televised committee hearing, followed by an episode where a reporter’s unexpected pause left him certain the room was about to collapse around him. He is seeking help to stop the night checks, to sit through a town hall without bracing for the next impact, and to find a way to exist in his own body without waiting for the other shoe to drop. He hopes to reclaim the steady focus he once commanded in the chamber, and he is most afraid that the silence will keep telling him he is not safe.
